doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Teaching Ornette and equal temperament
summary: Russell calls the Lenox students a gift, says Ornette showed him how to include everything, and says he only deals with equal temperament.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yes it is. So the Lenox, you were teaching the Lydian, and you had some tremendous students who – that must have been a lot of fun for you.
It was a challenge too, I bet.
No, that was a gift. Ornette played a meaningful role in his playing, because it was that that showed me how to include all that I – I had come up with a scale that could do all and everything.
You talk about equal temperament. It just occurred to me, and maybe this is not appropriate, but Ornette, here’s a guy who challenges the whole thing of the tempered
scale and all of that. So yes, challenge. That must have really been a challenge as well as . . .
I don’t deal with anything except equal temperament. So I’m not into certain forms of music that mess with temperament.
Go outside the laws. Yeah. There’s some chaos involved there, when you do that.
Well, it just doesn’t interest me.
